title: Hempstead Village Hall: Native Land Agreement Mural
summary: A twentieth-century mural of the 1643 land agreement raises questions about how Hempstead remembers Native people and colonial settlement.
address_label: Hempstead Village Hall, 99 James A. Garner Way, Hempstead
ancestral_territory_note: A Hempstead public artwork recalling Native representatives and the 1643 land agreement.
why_this_matters: Public art shapes which histories people encounter in everyday civic life. This mural invites a closer look at how Native people are represented, what a land agreement meant, and whose voices belong in the story.
introduction_title: A Land Agreement in Public Art
introduction_content: Robert Gaston Herbert’s twentieth-century mural in Hempstead Village Hall depicts the 1643 land agreement between Native representatives and English settlers. For generations, this commemorative scene formed the backdrop to village government.
history_content:
In April 2023, local reporting described the mural being concealed by a backdrop for televised village meetings. Archivist Regina G. Feeney urged that the artwork remain visible as an opportunity to learn about Long Island’s Indigenous roots.

The dispute concerns how public buildings display and interpret Native history. Keeping a painting visible also invites questions about its portrayal of land agreements and the Native perspectives a settlement scene may leave out.

Beyond a Single Transaction

The Merrick land records describe later negotiations, boundary disputes, and challenges to payment. A painted agreement should not be read as the end of Native presence or resistance.
whereintheworld_content: Village Hall is at 99 James A. Garner Way, formerly Nichols Court. The mural was reported covered in 2023. Contact Village Hall about viewing access before visiting specifically to see it.
